sections.markdown:
## C2 — Sign and signal confusables: shapes and colors, look-alike warning signs, and steady versus flashing versus arrow signals
Confusable pairs among sign families and signal lights, each tied to one manual page; knowledge-graph hints (group, difficulty, confusable pair) sit only in the trailing Why it matters line of each block.

FACT_ID: sec02-R01 | anchor: A01
A stop sign always requires a full stop, while a yield sign requires slowing and giving way, with a stop only when traffic or pedestrians make it necessary. [A01]
Why it matters: group prohibitive signs; confusable stop versus yield; difficulty easy.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec02-R02 | anchor: A01
The octagon means stop, the triangle means yield and the square red sign means Do Not Enter, so the shape alone tells you which rule applies. [A01]
Why it matters: group sign shapes; confusable octagon versus triangle versus square; difficulty easy.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec02-R03 | anchor: A06
A Reduced Speed Limit Ahead sign warns that a lower legal limit is coming, while an Advisory Speed sign only recommends a safe speed for a ramp or curve. [A06]
Why it matters: group speed signs; confusable coming speed limit versus advisory speed; difficulty medium.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec02-R04 | anchor: A02
A Right Lane Transit Only sign bars ordinary cars from going straight from that lane, while a Right Turns Permitted sign lets them enter it briefly to turn or park. [A02]
Why it matters: group transit lanes; confusable through movement versus brief right-turn use; difficulty hard.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec02-R05 | anchor: A03
A Do Not Pass sign forbids passing, while a No Turn on Red sign forbids turning until the light turns green. [A03]
Why it matters: group regulatory signs; confusable no passing versus no turn on red; difficulty easy.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec02-R06 | anchor: A03
A Center Lane Turn Only lane is shared by left-turning drivers from both directions, unlike a high occupancy vehicle lane, which is reserved by the number of people in the vehicle. [A03]
Why it matters: group special lanes; confusable two-way left-turn lane versus HOV lane; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec02-R07 | anchor: A04
A Curve sign and a Sharp Turn sign warn of what lies ahead, while a Chevron sign marks the sharp curve or direction change at the sign itself. [A04]
Why it matters: group curve signs; confusable advance warning versus at-the-spot marker; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec02-R08 | anchor: A05
A Merge sign means traffic will join your road from the side shown, while an Add Lane sign means the roads join with a new lane so nobody has to merge. [A05]
Why it matters: group lane signs; confusable merge versus added lane; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec02-R09 | anchor: A05
A Lane Reduction sign means your lane is ending and you must merge, which differs from a Two-Way Traffic Ahead sign, where a one-way road starts carrying oncoming traffic. [A05]
Why it matters: group lane signs; confusable lane ends versus two-way traffic begins; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec02-R10 | anchor: A05
A Winding Road sign means several turns or curves, while a Reversing Curves sign means one curve right followed by one curve left. [A05]
Why it matters: group curve signs; confusable many curves versus one reverse pair; difficulty easy.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec02-R11 | anchor: A07
Green signs guide you to exits, roads and cities, while brown signs point to historic, cultural and recreation sites. [A07]
Why it matters: group guide signs; confusable green guide versus brown recreation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0021]

FACT_ID: sec02-R12 | anchor: A08
A blue sign pointing to a hospital is a motorist service sign, the same family that shows fuel, food, lodging, rest areas, charging and accessible parking. [A08]
Why it matters: group service signs; confusable hospital route versus other directions; difficulty easy.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0022]

FACT_ID: sec02-R13 | anchor: A09
A steady red light means stop and stay stopped until it changes, while a flashing red light is treated like a stop sign. [A09]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable steady red versus flashing red; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec02-R14 | anchor: A09
Turning right on red onto a two-way road is allowed after a full stop, but a left turn on red is allowed only onto a one-way road going in the direction of the turn. [A09]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable right on red versus left on red; difficulty hard.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec02-R15 | anchor: A09
A steady yellow light tells you to stop before the intersection if you safely can, unlike a steady red light, which requires you to stop and stay stopped. [A09]
Why it matters: group signals; confusable steady yellow versus steady red; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0023]

FACT_ID: sec02-R16 | anchor: A10
A steady yellow arrow warns that the protected movement is ending, while a flashing yellow arrow allows the turn only after yielding to pedestrians and oncoming traffic. [A10]
Why it matters: group arrows; confusable steady yellow arrow versus flashing yellow arrow; difficulty hard.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0024]

FACT_ID: sec02-R17 | anchor: A10
A green arrow gives you the right of way for the movement shown, while a circular green light permits the movement but a left turn must still yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic. [A10]
Why it matters: group arrows; confusable protected green arrow versus permissive green ball; difficulty hard.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0024]
